newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu ally questions Israeli PM's leadership.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu ally questions Israeli PM's leadership.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu's political ally Natan Sharansky said a corruption scandal that rocked their government showed the prime minister had yet to prove he can lead the country.

The Israeli newspapers Yedioth Ahronoth and Maariv published interviews on Friday with Trade and Industry Minister Sharansky, a 49-year-old former Soviet dissident whose party has the power to bring down the 11-month-old government.

The attorney-general affair was one of a series of critical decisions -- including on peace, economic policies and the Israeli pullback from most of the West Bank town of Hebron -- which Sharansky said had been taken "in a strange way."

Asked what was the most critical thing he could say about Netanyahu, Sharansky said: "He thinks we're functionaries. Meanwhile he hasn't proved he knows how to lead a government. That's a huge shortcoming.
"What can be more serious than saying a prime minister doesn't know how to utilise his reservoir of ministers?"
Asked why that was, Sharansky said: "You must ask a psychologist."

Citing insufficient evidence, prosecutors said on Sunday they would not charge Netanyahu in an influence-peddling scandal despite what they said were "real suspicions" about his role in the short-lived appointment of an attorney-general in January.

Sharansky said: "The report is harsh, describing a series of serious matters. The lack of seriousness the prime minister showed at every stage of the process really cries out. In my eyes, that's a failed performance."
Sharansky said by staying in the government he hoped to accentuate Netanyahu's strong points and neutralise his shortcomings. He said he was convinced Netanyahu wanted to improve his performance.
"The moment we get the impression it's lip service, and I don't believe that will be the case, we will be out."

Sharansky's seven-member Yisrael ba-Aliya party this week persuaded Netanyahu to set up a committee to examine every appointment and government conduct. The party has enough clout to wipe out Netanyahu's 66-54 seat majority in parliament.

After nine years in Soviet prisons, Sharansky won his freedom in an East-West prisoner swap in 1986 and arrived in Israel to a hero's welcome. He emerged a big winner in Israeli elections last May after shunning politics for a decade.

Prosecutors say Shas religious party legislator Aryeh Deri, already on trial for corruption in another matter, should be charged in the attorney-general affair while the director-general of the prime minister's office, Avigdor Lieberman, faces further investigation.
